solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Meat dish in iron set alight

indicators.note: the meat dish sits in the chemical symbol, so that symbol is wrapped round it

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
lamb is a meat served as a dish

explanation.surface: A cook prepares lamb in an iron pan and then sets it alight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set alight' reads as part of the cooking scene, but it is the definition: the answer is the adjective for food doused in spirit and lit.
explanation.definitionFit: A culinary term borrowed from French for food covered in brandy and ignited, so literally flaming.

clue.text: Flyers run out fast, originally promoting Scottish site

indicators.note: promoting means moving up, and in a down clue that reverses the letters

parts.note: the RAF, the Royal Air Force, is made up of flyers

indicators.note: originally points to the first letters of run, out and fast

explanation.surface: Air force pilots run out fast, all promoting a site in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: RAF plus ROF, read upwards, gives FOR-FAR. Forfar is a town in Angus, Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Forfar is a Scottish town, so a named example of a place in Scotland.

clue.text: Vagrant tries to track source of cider, nicking one litre for cocktail

indicators.note: to track is to follow, so the anagram comes after
nicking means stealing, so the single litre abbreviation is taken away

parts.note: cider is made from apples

indicators.note: vagrant means wandering, so the letters of tries are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tramp tries to follow a cider supply, stealing a litre for a cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cocktail' suggests a drink, but a prawn cocktail is a starter; 'Vagrant' is the anagram signal, not the subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A starter such as a prawn cocktail is served before the main meal to whet the hunger.

clue.text: Country friend snatches to control setter

indicators.note: snatches means grabs and holds, so the friend word surrounds the other

parts.note: bud is informal for a friend
to run a business is to control it
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: A friend grabs the setter's controls in some country.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often call themselves I or ME; here the setter supplies the closing letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Burundi is a landlocked nation in East Africa, so an example of a sovereign state.

clue.text: Puzzle, when confronted, initially confuses — it's a killer

indicators.note: to be confronted is to be turned face to face, so the string of pieces is turned round and read backwards
initially points to the opening letter of the word confuses

parts.note: it's gives its letters without the apostrophe
the orca is the killer whale

explanation.surface: A puzzle that bewilders from the outset is described as a killer.
explanation.walkthrough: C (initially confuses), ITS and ORCA, read back to front under 'when confronted', give ACRO-STI-C.
explanation.definitionFit: A word puzzle in which initial letters of lines spell out a word, an example of the general category.

clue.text: Fizzy drinks, when poured out, becoming flatter

indicators.note: words poured out are spoken, so this signals a word that sounds alike

parts.note: Cokes are fizzy cola drinks

explanation.surface: Fizzy drinks poured out go flat, losing their sparkle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flatter' looks like 'more flat', the drinks going stale, but it is the verb: to sweet-talk.
explanation.definitionFit: To coax is to persuade by gentle sweet-talk, close to praising someone to win them over.

clue.text: Best work by Rice? Final stages of Evita musical

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
Tim Rice wrote the lyrics for Evita

indicators.note: final stages point to the last letter of each of Evita and musical

explanation.surface: Is the musical Evita lyricist Tim Rice's best work?
explanation.walkthrough: Tim Rice wrote the lyrics to Evita, so 'Rice' gives TIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Optimal means most favourable, the finest possible, so a synonym for top quality.

clue.text: Two singles with bat flicked part of leg

indicators.note: flicked means jerked about, so the letters are shuffled into a new order

parts.note: a single is one, I, so two of them give a pair of I's

explanation.surface: A batsman scoring two singles flicks the ball off his leg.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a single is one run; I is one, so two singles are II, mixed with BAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia is the shinbone, the larger bone of the lower limb.

clue.text: School discipline includes old English sport

indicators.note: includes means the discipline word holds the other letters inside

parts.note: caning was once a school punishment

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned school punishment includes an old English sport.
explanation.walkthrough: OE goes inside CANING.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddling a small boat is a water pastime, a recreational sport.

clue.text: Bear right beyond outskirts of Penzance to enter channel

indicators.note: to enter means these letters go inside the channel word

parts.note: a rut is a groove or channel

indicators.note: beyond places the abbreviation for right after the outskirts letters
outskirts are the outer edges, so only the first and last letters of Penzance count

explanation.surface: Directions for a hiker skirting the edge of Penzance, a Cornish seaside town, before heading into a channel.
explanation.walkthrough: PE plus R gives PER, which goes into RUT. Rupert Bear is a famous British cartoon bear.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert is the name of a well-loved British comic-strip bear, so a named example.

clue.text: Wild beast inhabits Caribbean — small number refuse to go there

indicators.note: something that inhabits a place lives inside it, so these letters go within

parts.note: WI stands for the West Indies, the Caribbean islands

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters of beast are rearranged

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for number, small because it is abbreviated

explanation.surface: A wild animal lives in the Caribbean, and a few people decline to visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refuse' looks like a verb but is the noun: rubbish. 'Wild' rearranges beast to ASTEB.
explanation.definitionFit: A receptacle for rubbish is literally the place where refuse is meant to be put.

clue.text: Forces welcomed top pilot in confrontation

indicators.note: welcomed means taken in, so the forces' letters surround the rest

parts.note: F is the physics symbol for force, doubled for the plural as in pp for pages
an ace is a top fighter pilot
in can mean of, as in 'one in ten' meaning one of ten

explanation.surface: The armed forces welcome their best pilot into a military showdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forces' looks military but gives two F's; 'in' standing for OF ('one in ten') is a loose Toughie equivalence.
explanation.definitionFit: A face-off is a direct standoff between opponents, so a synonym for a showdown.

clue.text: Newsreader Ford sits around time of broadcast close to the transmitting equipment

indicators.note: sits around means the presenter's name surrounds the time

parts.note: Anna Ford was a well-known British television newsreader
ten o'clock, the time of the long-running British news bulletin News at Ten

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A newsreader settles in around broadcast time, close to the studio's transmitting kit.
explanation.walkthrough: Anna Ford read the news on British TV; News at Ten is a nightly bulletin, hence TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerials that send or receive radio signals, so transmitting apparatus by another name.

clue.text: African savanna resident cut point for spear?

indicators.note: cut means the animal's name loses its final letter

parts.note: the impala is an antelope of the African savanna
E, east, is a compass point

explanation.surface: An African antelope wounded by the point of a hunter's spear.
explanation.walkthrough: IMPALA cut short gives IMPAL, then E (a compass point) is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To pierce something with a pointed weapon is to run it through, so spearing is the same act.

clue.text: One taking the plunge in cafe ordered head of eel

indicators.note: ordered means arranged, so the letters of in and cafe are put in a new order
head means the first letter of eel

explanation.surface: Someone orders an eel's head in a cafe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking the plunge' is the idiom for getting married, not diving; 'ordered' rearranges in cafe to FIANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking the plunge is an idiom for getting married, so a woman engaged is about to take it.

clue.text: Comedian from lace factory teased Gina

parts.note: to lace a drink is to spike it
a mill is a factory

indicators.note: teased as in hair teased out of shape, so the letters of Gina are rearranged

explanation.surface: A comedian from a lace-making factory taunts a woman called Gina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lace' looks like fabric but is the verb, to add alcohol secretly. Spike Milligan was a famous British-Irish comedian of The Goon Show.
explanation.definitionFit: Spike Milligan was a celebrated comic writer and performer, so a named example of a funny man.

clue.text: Study of trees unfulfilled graduate working alone extremely grubby

indicators.note: unfulfilled means emptied of its filling, so graduate loses everything between its first and last letters
working means in action, so the letters of alone are rearranged
extremely means at the extremes, the first and last letters of grubby

explanation.surface: An unfulfilled graduate studying trees works alone, extremely grubby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trees' looks botanical but means family trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Genealogy traces lines of descent, which are drawn up as family trees.

clue.text: A boy band consumed by ambition — to pick up the finest crumpet?

indicators.note: consumed by means eaten up, so the band's letters sit inside
to pick up means to lift, and in a down clue that reverses the letters

parts.note: an aim is an ambition
Bros was a British boy band of the late 1980s

explanation.surface: A boy band driven by ambition eyes the most attractive woman.
explanation.walkthrough: AIM read upwards gives MIA, which holds BROS. 'crumpet' is British slang for attractive people and also a griddle cake, hence food.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrosia is the food of the gods in Greek myth, so the finest food imaginable.

clue.text: Dancer often ran to gym, loosening up

indicators.note: loosening up suggests the letters are freed and reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A dancer often jogged to the gym to stretch and warm up.
explanation.definitionFit: Margot Fonteyn was a celebrated English prima ballerina, so a named example of a ballet performer.

clue.text: Mountain given lumpy interpretation in certain type of map

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters go within the map letters

parts.note: OS is the Ordnance Survey, Britain's official map-maker

indicators.note: an interpretation is a new reading, so the letters of lumpy are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mountain is drawn lumpy on a particular sort of map.
explanation.walkthrough: LYMPU, from lumpy, goes inside OS; Ordnance Survey maps are the standard British walking maps.
explanation.definitionFit: Olympus is the highest peak in Greece, home of the gods, so a named example.

clue.text: Set aside rake casually over soil

indicators.note: the rake letters are spread over the other word, enclosing it
casually means in a careless manner, so the letters of rake are rearranged

parts.note: to soil is to mar or spoil

explanation.surface: A gardener lays the rake aside, having casually raked the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soil' looks like earth but is a verb: to spoil. MAR goes inside EARK, from rake.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark funds is to reserve them for a purpose, so a synonym for setting them apart.

clue.text: One that's free when it is reversed

indicators.note: is reversed means the two-letter word in the middle is turned round

parts.note: something untied is loose or free
the word it, whose letters appear turned round in the free word

explanation.surface: A riddle: what is free when the word it is turned round?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a riddle about freedom; the definition is just 'One', in the sense of joined together.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined together as one, so united means acting as a single body.

clue.text: Left-winger to examine fault when shooting

parts.note: a red is a socialist or communist, someone on the political left
to eye something is to look it over

explanation.surface: A socialist inspects a shooting error, as if a political rifle range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shooting' suggests guns, but it means photography.
explanation.definitionFit: Flash photography can make pupils glow crimson in pictures, a well-known flaw of camera shots.

clue.text: Charlie caught in nude romps

indicators.note: in means the letter for caught sits within the rearranged letters
romps means frolics, so the letters of nude are jumbled

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A man named Charlie is caught frolicking naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like a name but is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlie is British informal for a foolish person, so a slow-witted pupil is one.

clue.text: Apple from tree's end branch overrun by pest

indicators.note: overrun by means swamped, so the pest word surrounds the other letters

parts.note: a pain is a pest, an annoying person

indicators.note: end points to the final letter of tree's, ignoring the possessive

parts.note: an arm is a branch, as of an organisation or river

explanation.surface: An apple tree whose branch tips are infested by a pest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end' takes the last letter of tree's, ignoring the possessive; a Pearmain is an old English apple variety.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pearmain is an old English variety of eating fruit from an orchard tree.

clue.text: See borders in floor covering

indicators.note: borders means the word for see forms the edges around the other

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see

explanation.surface: Look at the patterned borders on the floor covering.
explanation.walkthrough: LO (see, as in 'lo and behold') borders IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Linoleum is a hard-wearing flooring material, a familiar covering for kitchen floors.

clue.text: Run-down son with £25 handed over by relative

indicators.note: handed over is read as flipped over, so the slang word is reversed

parts.note: a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds
sis is short for sister, a relative

explanation.surface: A worn-out son is handed twenty-five pounds by a family member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run-down' looks like tired, but it is the noun: a summary. PONY is British slang for £25; reversed it gives YNOP.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief summary of the main points is a rundown, so a synonym in its noun sense.

clue.text: Half of tourists fancied eating a good hotpot abroad?

indicators.note: eating means the anagrammed letters take in the other two
fancied, as in fanciful or fancy, signals the letters are rearranged
half of means the first four of the eight letters of tourists

explanation.surface: Half a group of tourists fancied a hotpot on their trip abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: TOUR, the first half of tourists, is rearranged to ROUT, which takes in A and G.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragout is a French stew, so a hotpot from overseas, the question mark admitting the loose fit.

clue.text: Dislike leg-rest (odd bits missing) in French aeroplane

indicators.note: in means these letters go inside the French word

parts.note: avion is the French word for aeroplane

indicators.note: dropping the odd-numbered letters of leg-rest leaves the even ones

explanation.surface: A passenger dislikes the leg-rest, missing bits, in a French plane.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of leg-rest are E, R, S, which go into AVION.
explanation.definitionFit: An aversion is a strong distaste, so a synonym for a feeling of antipathy.

clue.text: Authorised dictionary contained a type of ox from the east

indicators.note: contained means the dictionary's letters hold the reversed animal

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary

indicators.note: in an across clue, from the east means reading right to left

parts.note: a yak is a long-haired ox of Tibet

explanation.surface: An authorised dictionary includes an entry for an ox from the east.
explanation.walkthrough: YAK reversed gives KAY, which goes into OED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given the go-ahead has been approved, the informal verb meaning sanctioned.
